messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Priya is a 23-year-old South Asian woman who works as a UX designer at a mid-sized tech firm in the Pacific Northwest. She is married and, until eight months ago, described herself as someone who moved through the world with quiet confidence — meticulous in her work, careful in her relationships, and proud of her attentiveness to others. That self-image fractured completely on a Tuesday evening in late autumn when, driving home from a client presentation, she failed to see a cyclist entering the intersection on her right. The collision happened in an instant she still cannot fully reconstruct: the sound of the impact, the way her car lurched, the figure on the pavement when she stepped out into the cold. The cyclist — a young man in a dark jacket, perhaps mid-twenties, carrying a messenger bag — sustained a fractured pelvis and a severe head injury. He survived, but Priya learned through subsequent legal proceedings that his recovery would be prolonged and uncertain. She had not been speeding. She had not been distracted. And yet she had not seen him, and that fact has become the central, immovable fact of her life.

In the weeks that followed, Priya returned to work because she did not know what else to do. The office, which had once felt like a space of creative absorption, became something she could barely tolerate. Her design work requires sustained visual attention — reviewing interface mockups, sitting in front of dual monitors for hours, navigating complex user-flow diagrams — and it was at her desk that the memories first began ambushing her. A colleague walking past her peripheral vision in a dark jacket, the particular angle of afternoon light through the office windows that matched the light that evening, even the sound of a bicycle courier in the lobby — any of these could pull her back to the intersection with a vividness she found unbearable. These triggers arrived without warning and without mercy, and it was their intrusion into her working hours that first drove Priya toward the strategies she has since come to rely on almost entirely.

When a memory or image surfaced at her desk, Priya began forcing her attention elsewhere — clenching her jaw and pushing the thought down, filling her mind with task lists or design specifications, anything to wall off what was trying to surface. She tried hard not to think about the trauma at all, treating each intrusion as something to be defeated through sheer will. Alongside this, she found herself returning compulsively to the moment of the accident in a different register: not reliving it, but analysing it, rehearsing every decision she made in the thirty seconds before impact, asking herself whether a different lane choice, a slower speed, a different departure time would have changed everything. This prevention rumination became a near-constant background process, running beneath her work and her conversations with her husband. What she did not recognise — and what has become clinically significant — is that both of these strategies kept the trauma perpetually active. The effort to suppress thoughts paradoxically sharpened her vigilance for anything that might trigger them, so that she arrived at work each morning in a state of low-grade hyperscanning, primed to detect dark jackets, bicycle shapes, the particular quality of overcast afternoon light. And the rumination, rather than resolving anything, rehearsed the emotional and sensory texture of the event so thoroughly that the triggers she was trying to suppress became only more potent and more numerous over time.

She has not driven since the night of the accident. She takes rideshares to work, but sitting in the passenger seat of a moving vehicle produces its own cascade, and she has begun declining client meetings that require travel. A colleague recently asked whether she was all right, having noticed she flinched visibly when a young man in a similar build to the cyclist walked through their open-plan office. Priya said she was tired.

It was her husband who finally persuaded her to seek help, after she woke him three nights in a row. What Priya most fears is that the person she injured is a version of someone she could encounter anywhere — and what she most hopes, though she can barely articulate it, is that she might someday be able to sit at her desk without feeling like a danger to the world.
